chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
title: Kirby calls him for a Washington nightclub job
summary: Kirby's postwar band was rebuilt; he offered Holmes two weeks in a Washington club and Holmes describes the group's precise light-classics style.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: But Kirby, he had some nice jobs to work on. He really did... He could get high-class work. The only thing about it, Kirby himself wasn't high class. Now, when I joined the band, he had a whole new band, because this was war times, the war was just over, and the war had broke up his band, his original band, with Procope and Billy Kyle and them... Well, Billy had come out of the Army; Billy was back with him. Buster Bailey wasn't with him. I think Bill Beason was drumming with him at the time.
Anyway, Kirby come to me. He says, "Charlie..."

Because he had tried to get me when I was with Cootie's band; two or three times he'd tried to get me. So he comes to me this time, he says, "Charlie, are you busy?" Well, at the time I wasn't busy doing nothing...or anything... I wasn't busy doing anything. And I said, "What's up? What's...?" He said, "Well, do you want to go down to Washington?" I said, "Well, I don't know. What is it?" He said, "A little nightclub down there. We'll be there a couple of weeks." I said, "Two weeks?" -- because two weeks sounded great to me. At the time, I think it was summertime or during that time, there wasn't a whole lot of work -- there wasn't a whole of gigs. So I says, "Okay." He gave me the name of the place.

But anybody that heard Kirby's band play, knows they played a different kind of music than any other kind of band. His is very precise. They were what they called "the biggest little band in the land," and believe me, when they put them three horns together, they sounded big too. It wasn't nothin' but a clarinet, a trumpet, a muted trumpet, and an alto saxophone. But when they got them arrangements, which Charlie made most of the arrangements...Charlie and Billy Kyle did most of the arranging. When they played the arrangements, boy, it sounded like a great big band. And they were playing all the light classics and one-thing-or-
another... Oh, I don't know, I can't name them. They had so many of them. They had a big, thick book.
